note.seg: Die archetype Überschrift will wahrscheinlich das ganze Stück bis 7, 1 umfassen. Nur B scheint sie auf Hu 1 allein zu beziehen, da er vor 2 eine besondere setzt, die aber 4 ff. nicht umschliesst

The archetypal heading is probably intended to cover the whole piece up to 7, 1. Only B seems to refer it to Hu 1 alone, since he places a separate heading before 2, which, however, does not cover 4 ff.

Da in diesem ganzen Stücke das Hundred nur in seiner gerichtlichen Funktion, nicht in militärischer oder wirtschaftlicher auftritt, so wähl ich als Überschrift das III Eg 5 gebrauchte Wort hundredgemot. Eigentümlich setzt, wohl aus Francolatein, dafür centenarius Cons, was bei anderen ‘Vorsteher des Hundred’ bedeutet

Since throughout this piece the hundred appears only in its judicial function, not in a military or economic one, I choose as heading the word hundredgemot used in III Eg 5. Cons peculiarly substitutes for it, probably from Frankish Latin, centenarius, which in other writers means ‘head of the hundred’

þæt hundred is translated ‘Hundertgericht’ (i.e. hundred court) by Liebermann in view of the fact that the hundred appears throughout only in its judicial function, and that the word hundredesgemot is employed in III Edg. 5 with reference to this law. In cap. 5, however, it is evidently the geographical district which is meant.

note.label: þæt
note.seg: þæt h. h. s. Ærest has been omitted in the text and added in the margin in the 12th cent.

This code survives in Old English in C.C.C.C., MS. 383, and in Latin in Quadripartitus and the appendix to Consiliatio Cnuti, in all three following two short texts, Blaseras “Incendiaries” and Forfang “(Legal) Seizure”, and hence coming from a collection in which the three texts had been assembled. The last two chapters, which have no connection with the code, may have been added to it by the same compiler, though no rubrics are added to them. This code is sometimes cited as I Edgar, but it could be earlier than Edgar’s reign, for the phrase in chap. 2 “as it was Edmund’s decree previously” does not necessarily imply that Edmund is dead. If it does mean this, however, this ordinance cannot be establishing the hundred as a new thing, for Edmund’s third code (III.2) refers to the hundred as an organised body. Even so, it could have been issued by Eadred or Eadwig, though, since no reference is ever made to these kings as law-givers, Edgar is the more likely king to have issued it. It would be the natural interpretation of the clause in chap. 2 to take it as referring to a previous king if one could be sure that the absence of a king’s name at the beginning of the code is a mere accident, for had it gone out in Edmund’s name one would have expected him to use the first person in chap. 2; but this is not conclusive, for changes in person are not uncommon. All that is certain, is that Edmund had issued a decree on the penalty for theft at some date before this ordinance. This decree has been lost, for there is no precise reference to the treatment of a thief in the extant laws of Edmund. Liebermann suggests that the ordinance used III Edmund, the code which refers to the hundred; there certainly seems a connection between III Edmund 3 and chap. 6 of the ordinance, but the borrowing could be the other way, or both codes may have used a common source. I do not think, therefore, that one can exclude the possibility that the ordinance did precede any other references to the hundred, though it cannot be proved that it did. There were certainly courts which met every four weeks before the time of this ordinance, and the places at which the hundreds held their meetings often have names which prove them to have been meeting-places from very early times. There is evidence from early times, too, of the assessment of the country in round figures of a hundred or multiples of a hundred hides, but no early evidence for administrative areas called hundreds or assessed at a hundred hides. While several of the midland counties are made up of hundreds which have this assessment, there is no such neat correspondence in the southern districts. It seems probable, therefore, that the institution of hundreds in the Midlands either was on a different principle from that current in the South, or took place at a much later date, when any original correspondence between the name and the assessment had in the South been obliterated by later developments. It seems simplest to regard this ordinance as part of a movement to secure some uniformity of administrative arrangements when, after the re-conquest of the Danelaw, the kings of Wessex were ruling all England. It might then be part of the same reorganisation of the Midlands that produced the modern shires. The name “hundred” for the smallest juridical area may have been an innovation of this reorganisation, applied for the sake of uniformity to divisions serving the same purpose in the South, even though these did not receive the same artificial assessment. This smallest juridical area seems originally to have administered from a royal estate. The code is edited by Liebermann, 1,192–5; and with English translation by Robertson, pp. 16–19, Thorpe, I, 258–61. [Her footnote 4: On the relation between the hundreds and the royal manors, see H.M.Cam, Eng. Hist. Rev., xlvii, 353–76. see also H.R.Loyn, in British Government and Administration: studies presented to S.B.Chrimes, pp. 1–15.]
